docs.title: Pathing
docs.text:
Pathing grants us the ability to locate a point through time, with its initial introduction as representing the location of the laser during Metal Additive Manufacturing. However, there is no reason why it couldn't be adapted to be utilized elsewhere, perhaps the source location of a water simulation.

The ComplexLinearPath, as we will use, is made up of a series of linear paths connected by waypoints. However, for simple shapes, two generators have been provided:

  • line_waypoint_generator(), and
  • circle_waypoint_generator(),

but these simply just generate waypoints in the format (x, y), (x, y, t), (x, y, z) or (x, y, z, t).

So, a list of coordinates can be generated, or self-made elsewhere. These are just meant to save you some time.

Since it's more complex, we will use circle_waypoint_generator() here, but you might ask yourself why we would ever want to split our line into a series of smaller lines, well that lies in geometry.add_path_shape() which we will get to later. However, in short, these shapes can be used to specifically sample more points in the region surrounding the 'path'. By splitting a line into smaller pieces both temporally and spatial we can better concentrate those points where they are needed.

Anyway, first lets locate the center of our domain. Since, we want our laser at the top of our shape, we fix the 'z' dimension.

center: tuple[float, float, float] = domain.center(fixed={"z": domain.max[2]})

The path in mind is two quarter-circles where the laser is off' as it traverses from one path the other. If you can't picture that, scroll down and look at the plot.

For, the first half:

waypoints1 = pinnjax.circle_waypoint_generator(
    center=center,
    diameter=0.018,  # m  -- smaller than the full shape domain.
    starting_angle=0,
    rotation_angle=90,
    time=pinnjax.Time(0, 1.3, 0.05),
    segments=30,  # 30 segments will result in 31 waypoints.
)

The parameters for this function should be straightforward, but in case it isn't, we are rotating around the outer edge of a circle centered at the top and center of our domain, with a diameter of 0.0225, starting at 0° on the Unit Circle and moving 90°.

If degrees scare you, you can use radians instead, just set the parameter:

  • angle_units = "radians".

This arc is not smooth, but rather made up of 30 segments. The time will determine how fast our laser is moving. These calculations are all done internally, but a speed can be inputted instead, which is a uniform linear speed. Or nothing and you're left with purely spatial waypoints until a later step.

Now lets draw the second half, this time starting at 270° and moving -90°:

waypoints2 = pinnjax.circle_waypoint_generator(
    center=center,
    diameter=0.018,  # m
    starting_angle=270,
    rotation_angle=-90,
    time=pinnjax.Time(1.7, 3, 0.05),
    segments=30,
)

Now, lets combine the two.

waypoints = jnp.vstack((waypoints1, waypoints2))

Remember, these are both just lists of waypoints, so the once the Path is generated the connection line between the two will be included automatically. However, we planned on turning it off, so let's do that.

active: dict[str, list | int] = {"off": 31}

The first quarter has 30 segments, the second has 30, but the connection becomes segment number 31, for a total of 61 segments.

Now let's generate the path_config.

path_config = pinnjax.ComplexLinearPathConfig(
                            waypoints=waypoints, 
                            is_temporal=True, 
                            active=active
)

Naturally, we give it our generated waypoints, but what else?

First, since waypoints could be (x, y), (x, y, t), (x, y, z) or (x, y, z, t) the configuration initialization has no way of knowing if the given waypoints already include time, thus is_temporal simply indicates that the final column is time. If it wasn't already temporal we could also provide a speed here and the temporal portion would be generated.

Next, is active, which we have already used to turn off segment number 31, but we could also turn off multiple sections like active = {"off": [20, 31, 50]}. Naturally, you shouldn't pick numbers greater than the total number of segments in your waypoints. If for some reason you find yourself turning off a large number of segments, it might be more convenient to only turn on the relevant segments active = {"on": [20, 31, 50]}. But, remember, the path 'source' is always moving, particularly because it is mimicking a real world mechanical device, so even off segments will have a calculated travel time.

Then simply,

path = pinnjax.create_path(path_config)

pinnjax.create_path() identifies which of the three types of path config was provided LinearPathConfig, CirclePathConfig, or ComplexLinearPathConfig, and creates the appropriate Path: LinearPath, CirclePath, and ComplexLinearPath, respectively.

By creating a Path, we now have access to a number of methods, particularly helpful for verifying and visualizing our work. The previous steps internally included a number of verifications, such as ensuring the time times are consecutive, speeds are positive, etc... But, it didn't know the SpatialDomain it was attached to, so next let's validate the path on the domain.

path.validate(domain)

The main check here is making sure that the path remains within the domain, if not you might have some sampling problems later.

Next, lets visualize our Path.

path.draw(domain=domain)

Figure

It even shows when the 'source' is "off".

Remember when we made used the circle_waypoint_generator(), here is a way to verify that we used the correct degrees. Though, sorry degree-aphobes, no radians here.

path.draw(
    domain=domain,
    show_angle_axes=True,
    center=domain.center(fixed={"z": 0}),  # let's put it at the bottom.
)

Figure

A picture tells a thousand words, but a video is a bunch of pictures.

So, let's really verify using an animation. This also helps to verify the speeds, assuming you keep that in mind when choosing the number of frames and fps, as well as the fact that different .gif viewers might play back .gifs at different speeds.

path.animate(domain=domain)

Figure

docs.title: Geometry
docs.text:
Enough fun, back to business. Let's create a geometry from our SpatialDomain.

obb = domain.to_obb()

Since we are in 3 Dimensions we should use the BoundedBox.

A BoundedBox is defined as 7 shapes:

  • A Box, and,
  • 6 Rectangles on each edge

Plus, an additional Box if initial=True.

geometry = pinnjax.BoundedBox(*obb, times=time)

docs.title: Sampling
docs.text:
Since, the 1D diffusion example used "point_count" - SobolSampler, let's mix it up for a moment and use "grid_resolution" - UniformSampler. We can swap this out later to really highlight the modularity of PINN-JAX.

method = pinnjax.UniformSampler(mode="grid_resolution")

Let's pick some resolutions per shape. Remember, the temporal sampling is based on the step set in the Time. Unlike with SobolSampler which uses the step as a multiplier, there's no funny business here, the identical points are sampled throughout time.

# reminder, the domain was (0.028, 0.028, 4e-3)
resolutions = [2e-3, 2e-3, 2e-3, 2e-3, 2e-3, 2e-3, 2e-3]
# resolutions are in the same units as the domain, not relative to it.

Since they are all the same, we could also just do resolutions = 2e-3, or have assigned it directly to the method.

geometry.add_path_shape(path, radius=[2e-3, 2e-3, 4e-3])
# The `radius` is defined as the distance from the path, not the total size.

Additional Shapes are added under the 'source' as it travels through time. This is only currently available for BoundedBox, and the additional Shapes are assumed to be touching the top surface, thus it makes a ComplexShape, defined by an interior Box and a Rectangle at the top surface. This way you can assign the correct residuals to the correct points.

resolutions.extend([1e-3, 1e-3])

Make note: you will sample at this resolution for all segments. The more segments you add, the more points this will result in because the path shapes overlap. Granted, this is only a major concern if using "point_count", since the other two scale by domain size, and with more segments, the segments themselves are smaller.

Confused? Probably. Pictures solve everything.

geometry.draw(show_path=True)

Figure

Now let's sample.

geometry.sample(method, resolutions)

Everyone likes pictures.

geometry.draw(show_path=True, show_samples=True)

Figure

Now, that the points are sampled, we actually don't need all of those Shapes, in-fact keeping them will complicate things because we will need to assign a residual for each of them, and during 'training' we will need to loop through all of them.

Currently, we have a ComplexShape inside our ComplexShape, which was convenient for assigning samples, but they are unnecessary. .unpack(), well, unpacks the internal ComplexShape. Then, flatten=True replaces all compatible shapes with one all encompassing Shape. A 'compatible' Shape in this case means all the children' have the same Shape, Residual, and Loss.

geometry.unpack(flatten=True)

We could've 'unpacked' and 'flattened' prior to sampling, but the points would be sampled into the larger all encompassing shape, defeating the point of the localized path shape samples.

Once again, for visual clarity:

geometry.draw(show_path=True, show_samples=True)

Figure

And here we can see the number of samples total. Notice the additional Box and Rectangle. We will need to remember them when we assign losses and residuals.

geometry.print_samples()

Shape 1 (Box): 4704 collocation points
Shape 2 (Rectangle): 336 collocation points
Shape 3 (Rectangle): 336 collocation points
Shape 4 (Rectangle): 336 collocation points
Shape 5 (Rectangle): 336 collocation points
Shape 6 (Rectangle): 2352 collocation points
Shape 7 (Rectangle): 2352 collocation points
Shape 8 (Box): 8384 collocation points
Shape 9 (Rectangle): 2096 collocation points

As always, videos are pretty cool.

geometry.animate(show_samples=True, show_path=True)

Figure

And here is a version where the points from all timesteps are collectively shown.

geometry.animate(show_samples=True, show_path=True, additive=True,)

Figure

You'll notice the general uniform points seems to flash in and out, this is because the general points are sampled at a different temporal discretization as the points added from the path shape. To clarify, it is the same 'step_size', but the start and end points are dictated by the segmentation, so the time-discretization is not necessarily aligned.

In the case of UniformSampler, it this only effects the additionally sampled points since all points are repeated at each time step in the uniform case

docs.title: Hyperparameter Exploration
docs.text:
For something a bit more interesting, let's try this again, but with the SobolSampler.

Despite the fact that I've recreated the geometry and rewritten the function calls the only change in the following entire section is changing the word 'Uniform' to 'Sobol'.

This is the point of this modular framework -- to best facilitate hyperparameter exploration.

geometry = pinnjax.BoundedBox(*obb, times=time)
method = pinnjax.SobolSampler(mode="grid_resolution")

resolutions = [2e-3, 2e-3, 2e-3, 2e-3, 2e-3, 2e-3, 2e-3]

geometry.add_path_shape(path, radius=[2e-3, 2e-3, 4e-3])
resolutions.extend([1e-3, 1e-3])

geometry.sample(method, resolutions)
geometry.unpack(flatten=True)

geometry.draw(show_path=True, show_samples=True)

Figure

geometry.print_samples()

Shape 1 (Box): 1568 collocation points
Shape 2 (Rectangle): 112 collocation points
Shape 3 (Rectangle): 112 collocation points
Shape 4 (Rectangle): 112 collocation points
Shape 5 (Rectangle): 112 collocation points
Shape 6 (Rectangle): 784 collocation points
Shape 7 (Rectangle): 784 collocation points
Shape 8 (Box): 2815 collocation points
Shape 9 (Rectangle): 719 collocation points

geometry.animate(show_samples=True, show_path=True)

Figure

geometry.animate(show_samples=True, show_path=True, additive=True)

Figure

You should notice two things, first, that the SobolSampler results in less points even with the same resolutions, this is because the SobolSampler using "grid_resolution" attempts to calculate the number of 'equivalent' uniform points, by estimating the necessary uniform points and then reducing those values by a factor dependent on the dimensionality of the sample space. The second thing you'll notice is, despite that, the Sobol points seem to better fill the spatial domain, which is the intended point of Sobol sampling.

docs.title: 1D Diffusion
docs.text:
The full runnable script can be found at examples/public/diffusion.py on GitHub.

Note

It's recommended to read all the examples in order, as previously explained portions won't be as thoroughly explained in later examples, and vice-versa concerning the content provided in this example.

Note

Some of the function calls, particularly for the visualizations have been simplified from the call which generated the image, this is to highlight only the necessary parameters for these functions.

docs.title: Includes
docs.text:
• Purely Physics-Informed
  • Time-Dependent 1D Dimensional Problem (BoundedBox)
  • Sobol Point Sampling (SobolSampler)
  • Feedfoward Neural Networks (FNN)
  • Hard Constraints (HardConstraint)

docs.title: Problem Description
docs.text:
Here we train a simple time-dependent 1D diffusion problem on \([-1, 1]\) from \(t = 0\) to \(t = 1\):

\[ u_t = D u_{xx}, \quad u(x, 0) = \sin\left(\frac{n\pi}{2}(x + 1)\right), \quad u(\pm 1, t) = 0. \]

With defaults,

diffusion_coefficient = 0.25  # D
mode = 5                      # n

Feel free to experiment with different values.

docs.title: Domain
docs.text:
First, we need to define the domain space of our problem, both spatially and temporally. Both are initialized similarly to the problem statement, using SpatialDomain and Time, respectively.

time = pinnjax.Time(min=0, max=1, step=0.1)
# from 0s to 1s with a 0.1s time-step
# the time-step is used exclusively for sampling.
domain = pinnjax.SpatialDomain(min=(-1,), max=(1,), times=time)
# if the problem isn't time-dependent use times=None or omit.

As the comment states, the discretization step in Time only factors into collocation point sampling, in certain instances, which will be explained in further detail later.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
The order of this next section is a bit incongruent for tutorial purposes, but next we define the Optimization object, containing:

  • InputTransformation;
  • OutputTransformation;
  • HardConstraint.

None of which are necessary to the functionality of the model, but can modify and potentially improve the results the model -- optimizing it.

An InputTransformation is applied to the inputs as a pre-processing step, such as:

  • Normalization, for instance NormalizationBetweenNeg1and1 or NormalizationBetween0and1

An OutputTransformation is applied after the model output as a post-processing step.

And, finally, HardConstraint, which isn't as self-explanatory as the previous two, is applied following the OutputTransformation with the express purpose of improving model performance.

When training a model using data, physics, or both, we instill soft constraints on the model. While ideally a trained model perfectly adheres to physical-reality, we know some amount of error will always exist, thus soft constraints.

With hard constraints we mathematically modify the raw model output \(\mathcal{N}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\) to adhere with physics.

\[\hat{u} = g(\mathbf{x}) + (\phi(\mathbf{x}) \cdot (\mathcal{N}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) - g(\mathbf{x})))\]

where:

\[\phi(\mathbf{x}) = 1 - \exp\left( -\frac{d(\mathbf{x}, \Gamma)}{\tau} \right)\]

or more simply, is a weighting function which blends to zero as the input point \(\mathbf{x}\) nears the constrained manifold \(\Gamma\). In the case of the initial condition, \(d\left(\mathbf{x}, \Gamma_{\mathrm{IC}}\right)=|t-t_{\min}|\).

Thus, in the original prediction formula \(\hat{u}\) we are left with only \(g(\mathbf{x})\) at \(\Gamma\).

Therefore, by defining \(g(\mathbf{x})\), or initial_condition_fn(), we can hard constrain our predictions.

def initial_condition_fn(pt):
    # pt[0] is x, pt[-1] is t
    return jnp.sin(mode * (jnp.pi / 2) * (pt[0] + 1))

# Hard Constraint on the Initial Condition
hard_ic = pinnjax.HardArrayInitialConstraint(
                times=time,
                initial_condition=initial_condition_fn
)

HardArrayInitialConstraint as been predefined for this purpose. As it's name implies initial_condition can be either an Array or a function, which was used here. A scalar version also exists, HardScalarInitialConstraint, as well as a version for spatial coordinates, HardDirichletConstraint.

Given the mathematics restrictions, the pre-made functions are limited to Dirichlet boundaries.

# Define the Optimization Object
optimization = pinnjax.Optimization(
    # Input Transformations
    input_transformation=pinnjax.NormalizationBetweenNeg1and1(domain=domain),
    # Output Transformations
    output_transformation=None, 
    # Hard Constraints 
    hard_constraint=(hard_ic, ), 
)

Currently, you're limited to ONE InputTransformation and ONE OutputTransformation, but multiple HardConstraint which are applied consecutively. If the constraints are compatible with each other they will be combined to avoid them fighting each other.

These optimizations are not necessary, one can either set the parameter to None, which is the default value. Or, equivalently, set it to an empty Optimization object: optimization = pinnjax.Optimization(), which sets each optimization to an identity version of itself.

Considering the complexity of the problem, we opt for a relatively small Feedfoward Neural Network. There are other predefined architecture options, but they aren't suitable nor necessary for this use-case.

All NeuralNetwork have been written utilizing the equinox package as a base.

# Define the topology (specific to FNN) [input, layer .... layer, output]
topology = (2, 8, 8, 8, 8, 1)  # [input: x, t] [output: u]

# Define the Activation Object. 
# Currently, all interior layers get the same activation.
activation = pinnjax.Activation(jax.nn.tanh)
# Look at the jax.nn documentation for available options.
# If the selected option has args or kwargs:
# activation = pinnjax.Activation(jax.nn.gelu, kwargs={"approximate": False})

# Initialize the Model 
model = pinnjax.FNN(
    domain,
    topology,
    activation,
    optimization=optimization,  # optional parameter defaults to None
    initialization=None,        # optional parameter defaults to None
)

The Activation function, as noted, is applied to all interior layers, and is simply a wrapper for an jax.nn activation.

The initialization, or Initialization, is not utilized here, but refers to the initial state of the random weights and biases. The object is, again, simply a wrapper for jax.nn.initializers.

Here is a visual representation of the FNN, with

  • 2 inputs (\(x\), \(t\)),
  • 4 Hidden Layers with 8 nodes, and
  • 1 output (\(\hat{u}\)).

Figure

Hence, topology = (2, 8, 8, 8, 8, 1).

docs.title: Geometry
docs.text:
A time-dependent BoundedLine contains FOUR interior primitive Shape objects:

  • A temporal Line, two Dot, and an initial Line.
geometry: ComplexShape = pinnjax.BoundedLine(
    origin = domain.min,
    end = domain.max,
    times=time,
    initial=True,
)
# Other options include BoundedBox (3D) and Bounded Rectangle (2D), or you can
# make your own pinnjax.ComplexShape() class, though naturally you'll have to
# write all additional features. There's also Hypercube which allows for higher-
# dimensional domains, which aren't necessarily spatial-temporal.

# initial=True means a shape will be added to the ComplexShape only at t=0.
# if you forget to add this initial shape, it can be added later with: 
#    geometry.add_initial(). 
# Since we are hard constraining our initial conditions, this isn't strictly
# necessary, but showing the model initial points, even when using hard
# constraints, during training has been shown to increase stability.
  • A 2D problem uses BoundedRectangle.
  • A 3D problem uses BoundedBox.

docs.title: Sampling
docs.text:
We now need to sample points within all of these shapes. Currently, the only SamplingMethod is the SobolSampler so we use that here, but feel free to write your own.

method = pinnjax.SobolSampler(mode="point_count")

npoints = [1000, 20, 20, 10]

# Sample:
geometry.sample(method, sampling_values=npoints)

The results, while underwhelming for a 1D Geometry, can be plotted with .draw() method.

>>> geometry.draw(show_samples=True)

Figure

geometry.print_samples()

Shape 1 (Line): 1000 collocation points
Shape 2 (Dot): 20 collocation points
Shape 3 (Dot): 20 collocation points
Shape 4 (Line): 10 collocation points

The SobolSampler samples from the unit-hypercube following a pseudo-random sequence in an effort to most efficiently fill the sample space. In the case of our time-dependent Line, this is a 2D-hypercube. Therefore, while the visualization shows samples throughout the geometry spatially, they are also spread throughout time. This is also why we've opted to sample 20 points at each Dot -- they aren't in the same place in time.

The SobolSampler has three modes which determine how sampling_values is interpreted, in order to determine how many points to sample:

  • "point_count": uses the scalar value.
  • "grid_resolution": treats the value as a resolution and calculates the equivalent grid distribution setting the number of samples as a factor of this value dependent on sample dimensionality
  • "density": treats the value as a density and calculates the length, area or volume of the sample space.

For both "grid_resolution" and "density" the calculated values are simply spatial. The temporal component is taken into account using the step parameter set in an earlier section as part of Time. They, simply, multiply the calculated value by the number of discrete time steps.

Since, we've used "point_count" this isn't factored in at all.

docs.title: Residuals
docs.text:
Now to put the PINN in PINN-JAX.

We need to define the Residuals for our model. A residual is the difference between the predicted value of our model \(\hat{u}\) and the "truth", a simple subtraction. In a data-driven network, both halves are readily available, with the "truth" contained in a dataset. However, for physics-informed neural networks, we need to calculate the "truth" throughout training dependent on the current point and prediction. Slightly more complex.

In this case,

  • the PDE residual is \(\hat{u} - D u_{xx}\),
  • the BC residual is \(\hat{u} - 0\), and
  • the IC residual is \(\hat{u}(\mathbf{x}, 0) - g(\mathbf{x})\).

The equations are less complex than they appear. The complexity comes from the integration with JAX.

  • ._residual(): handles a single point.
  • ._residuals(): handles a group of points using vmap.
  • __call__(): is called during train().

Within this formulation DifferentialOperators are used, which provide some simple, pre-defined functions for derivatives with JAX-efficiency in-mind, but their use isn’t mandatory. What is mandatory, however, is providing a __call__() function with a points and ops parameter, regardless of whether it is used.

# PDE
# Make a subclass of pinnjax.PartialDifferentialEquation
class Diffusion(pinnjax.PartialDifferentialEquation):
    # define:
    #     an __init__,
    #     a _residual (one point at a time),
    #     a _residuals() (vmapped)
    #     and an @eqx.filter_jit __call__()

    # the _residual, _residuals, and __call__ must have the same inputs as here.
    def __init__(self, diffusion_coeff: float = 1e-3):
        self.diffusion_coeff = diffusion_coeff

    def _residual(self, u: Array, ops: pinnjax.DifferentialOperators) -> Array:
        u_t = ops.evolution_derivative(u)
        u_xx = ops.laplacian(u)  # in 1D this is d^2 u / dx^2
        return u_t - self.diffusion_coeff * u_xx

    def _residuals(self, 
                   points: Array,
                   ops: pinnjax.DifferentialOperators
            ) -> Array:
        vm = jax.vmap(lambda p: self._residual(p, ops), in_axes=0)
        return jnp.nan_to_num(vm(points), nan=1e-6, posinf=1e6, neginf=-1e6)

    @eqx.filter_jit
    def __call__(self, 
                points: Array,
                ops: pinnjax.DifferentialOperators
            ) -> Array:
        return self._residuals(points, ops)

# BC
class DiffusionBC(pinnjax.BoundaryCondition):
    # same deal here, but for a subclass of pinnjax.BoundaryCondition
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()

    def _residual(self, 
                points: Array,
                ops: pinnjax.DifferentialOperators
            ) -> Array:
        u_val = ops.T(points)
        return u_val

    def _residuals(self, 
                points: Array, 
                ops: pinnjax.DifferentialOperators
            ) -> Array:
        vm = jax.vmap(lambda p: self._residual(p, ops), in_axes=0)
        return jnp.nan_to_num(vm(points), nan=1e-6, posinf=1e6, neginf=-1e6)

    @eqx.filter_jit
    def __call__(self, 
                points: Array, 
                ops: pinnjax.DifferentialOperators
            ) -> Array:
        return self._residuals(points, ops)

# IC
# Since we are hard constraining our Initial Conditions this isn't strictly 
# necessary, but it helps to make sure it's working.
class DiffusionIC(pinnjax.InitialCondition):
    # This particular class utilizes the predefined functions of the parent
    # InitialCondition class but in effect it has the same format as the other 2
    # types. 
    # Functionally, all 3 (PDE, BC, IC) are identical in function, but they are 
    # separated for the purpose of weighted loss functions and adaptive weights.
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__(lambda pt: jnp.sin(mode * (jnp.pi / 2) * (pt[0] + 1)))

With our Residuals define them, we can assign them to our geometry using .assign_residuals(). The list of residuals should follow same order as the generated shapes, as was the case when sampling.

initial_condition = DiffusionIC()
boundary_condition = DiffusionBC()
pde = Diffusion(diffusion_coefficient)

# Assign the Residuals to the shape.
# Again here you need to remember the number of shapes you have and their order.
residuals: list[pinnjax.Residual] = [
    pde,
    boundary_condition,
    boundary_condition,
    initial_condition,
]
# Assign them:
geometry.assign_residuals(residuals)

Now the same for Loss.

While, a Residual is the difference between the prediction and the "truth". The Loss is the metric applied to it, such as:

  • Mean Error (ME): ResidualMeanError
  • Mean-Squared Error (MSE): ResidualMSError
  • Mean-Absolute Error (MAE): ResidualMAError
  • ...

However, as with everything in PINNJAX, you are not limited to what has been created, simply create a subclass of Loss, define your CustomLoss and all systems will function as normal.

# Assign the Loss function
geometry.assign_loss(pinnjax.ResidualMSError())

Rather than a list, we assign all Shapes the same Loss. However, it is possible to assign individual Loss by providing a list. Similarly, a single Residual can be used in .assign_residuals() to assign all Shapes the same Residual.

Multiple Residuals or Losses can be assigned to the same Shape.

geometry.assign_residuals([
        [pde1, pde2],
        bc
    ])

docs.title: Training
docs.text:
With the Model, Geometry, Residuals, Losses, and Samples, all defined, all that is left is to train.

But first, we need an Optimizer. Like Activation, Initialization, mentioned in Model, this also is a wrapper, in this case for optax.

Here Adam is used as it is often considered one of the "default" optimizer, and, thus, a good starting point for hyperparameter optimization. A different optimizer, from this list can be slotted in instead, but depending on the complexity of their output and call parameters, they aren't all guaranteed to work.

scheduler = 0.001
optimizer = pinnjax.Optimizer(
    optax.adam,
    kwargs={"learning_rate": scheduler, "b1": 0.9, "b2": 0.999},
)

We aren't limited to using a scalar value for learning_rate, we can instead use a learning rate scheduler which updates throughout the training period. More information about these, and other features, can be found in the docs for optax.

scheduler = optax.exponential_decay(
    init_value=1e-2,
    transition_steps=100,  # decay every 100 epochs
    decay_rate=0.95,  # 5% reduction each time
    end_value=1e-5,  # don't go below this
)

Lastly, the Training object, which contains all important information about the training configuration.

training = pinnjax.Training(
    optimizer,
    epochs=20000,  # set the number of epochs
    # everything after here is optional and has a default value.
    use_adaptive_weights=False,
    # automatically update the weighting of the
    # multi-objective loss function
    adaptive_alpha=0.9,
    # how much of current weights effects new calculation.
    update_weights_every=1000,  # how often to update weights
    update_weights_after=250,
    # when to start updating weights (starting very early is
    # unstable)
    train_mode="class",  # type or class type divides the
    # losses (for the purpose of adaptive weights) into
    # Diffusion, pde2, DiffusionBC, bc2, etc... class divides
    # into PDE, BC, IC
    balance_magnitudes=False,
    # since the expected residual loss of one residual might
    # be very different from another this aims to allow the
    # model to learn all objectives, by pulling the losses
    # closer in magnitude.
    magnitude_clip=1e-2,
    # limit of how much the loss can be modified.
    early_stopping=True,
    # if loss has converged, whether to stop training early.
    rel_tolerance=0.0001,
    # compared to the current best model, how much better
    # is the new model (relatively)
    patience=1000,
    # how many epochs without improvement (better than
    # the relative tolerance) before stopping
)

And now we train.

updated_model = pinnjax.train(
    model,
    geometry,
    training,
    verbosity=50,  # how often (in epochs) to print the results (loss).
    print_mode="class",  # same as train_mode but for the print.
)

Throughout training, the loss is saved to the geometry and can be plotted with the .plot_loss() method.

geometry.plot_loss(
    save=SAVE,
    mode="type",
    show_best_epoch=True,
    show=SHOW,
    save_location=model_path,
    save_format=".png"
)

Figure

This plot is useful, but it also allows me to visually explain some the parameters from earlier. Firstly, early_stopping which is why despite epochs = 20000 the training stopped after 8831. This is because the model failed to improve by more than 0.01% (rel_tolerance=0.0001) for more than 1000 consecutive epochs (patience=1000).

Total Time    = 46.781s
Final Loss:
    Class:
        Diffusion = 0.00361989
        DiffusionBC = 0.000168309
        DiffusionIC = 0
    Type:
        PartialDifferentialEquation = 0.00361989
        BoundaryCondition = 0.000168309
        InitialCondition = 0

docs.title: Saving
docs.text:
Both for model reuse and result tracking, it is important to both save the results and the model itself. The first function .save_model(), saves the model weights, as its name suggests, which allows us to use .load_model() at a later date. However, automatic model loading is only confirmed to work properly for FNN models. In order to load a model you need to reconstruct the same model, including the exact same Optimization. Thus, .load_model() is not strictly necessary, as it is merely attempting to read the model folder, and what was saved using .save_configuration().

# now we just save the model. this function will also save a .json file
# which will make it much easier to use this model for predicting later.
model_path = pinnjax.save_model(updated_model, path=model_path, return_path=True)
# since we have a return variable 'model_path' we need return_path = True, but
# since we already have model_folder as Path, it's not necessary. in this case
# model_path == model_folder.

# you might have noticed config.LOGGER throughout the code. Using logging is
# more computationally efficient than using print() and it gives us the option
# save everything printed to the console to a .log file for looking at later.
# will you ever want to look at it? probably not, but it's nice to know it's
# there. The .log file will only be generated if you've set up the logger,
# at the start of the script, such as pinnjax.config.setup_logger().

# however, the default save location is just directly next to the script being
# used, which is a bit silly when we are saving all the results. this function
# moves that file to the model_path we just made.
if model_path is not None:
    pinnjax.config.relocate_log(model_path)

# this is where we save important training parameters, so in the event the model
# is successful (or unsuccessful), we will have record of each parameter used.
# that being said, it can only save what you tell it to.
pinnjax.save_configuration(
    model_path,
    timing=timing,
    geometry=geometry,
    model=model,
    training=training,
)

docs.title: Prediction
docs.text:
Since this was a purely-physics-informed neural network, the true solution never came into the picture, however, for the purpose of verifying out results its rather important.

Luckily, there is an analytical solution:

\[ u(x, t) = \exp\left(-\left(\frac{n\pi}{2}\right)^2 D t\right) \sin\left(\frac{n\pi}{2}(x + 1)\right). \] 
def analytic_solution(_x, t, _mode=1, D=1e-3):
    """Analytical solution for IC.

    u(x,t) = exp(- (pi/2)^2 * D * t) * sin(pi/2 * (x+1))
    """
    k = _mode * (np.pi / 2)
    return np.exp(-(k**2) * D * t) * np.sin(k * (_x + 1))

Of course, the existence of an analytical solution negates any purpose for training a surrogate, but this is a simple example after all.

A LineGrid is the evaluation mesh. Considering the sampled collocation points are sparsely spanning the entire spatial-temporal domain, we can instead sample uniform points exclusively for prediction.

# Grid Construction Rather than our Sobol points, we can use 
# our model to predict using a simple grid. 
# 
# Here is a predefined LineGrid, since this is a 1D problem, you are naturally 
# limited to a LineGrid, but other options include RectangularGrid, 
# RectangularGrid3D, and ComparisonGrid. A 2/3D Domain can use a lower 
# dimensional grid by the fixed_coordinates.
grid = pinnjax.LineGrid(
    domain=domain, axis="x", num_points=100, time_range=(0, 1), num_times=100
)
# inputs should be self-explanatory.

# predict_evolution() is a wrapper around the function `.predict()`
# which loops through the time-steps of the Grid.
preds = pinnjax.predict_evolution(_model, _grid)  
# shape: (num_times, num_points)

As seen in the full script, a specific wrapper function was written to plot both the analytical and predicted solution simultaneously however, within predict_evolution() is called with the trained model and this grid.

Where we can now see our visualized results.

Figure

However, this is not where the story ends, but rather the beginning.

docs.title: Hyperparameter Optimization
docs.text:
The purpose of hyperparameter optimization is to modify the parameters in such a way to optimize the results. While there are many, much more advanced and methodical ways to achieve this, none of which have been fully implemented into PINNJAX, here we will attempt 'Random Search', and simply just modify on parameter at a time, utilizing expert knowledge and luck.

First, let's change the Optimizer from Adam to LBFGS. Since each epoch of LBFGS is significantly more computationally expensive compared to Adam, we've also simultaneously reduced the number of epochs to 1000.

optimizer = pinnjax.Optimizer(
    optax.lbfgs, 
    kwargs={
        "learning_rate": scheduler,
        "memory_size": 50,  # default 10
        "linesearch": optax.scale_by_zoom_linesearch(
            max_linesearch_steps=75,  # default 15
            initial_guess_strategy="one",
        ),
    },  # recommended by documentation
)

Figure

Total Time    = 15m: 46.685s
Final Loss:
    Class:
        Diffusion = 0.0121203
        DiffusionBC = 0.000849124
        DiffusionIC = 0
    Type:
        PartialDifferentialEquation = 0.0121203
        BoundaryCondition = 0.000849124
        InitialCondition = 0

It appears this version is slightly worse, both visually and numerically, and took significantly longer. However, in particular, the error seems most visually apparent at the boundaries. Considering, we've already managed to perfectly hard constrain the initial condition, it might be worth it to constrain the two Dirichlet boundaries, as well.

So, let's return to the original optimizer, Adam, and add some additional constraints.

hard_ic = pinnjax.HardArrayInitialConstraint(
                times=time,
                initial_condition=initial_condition_fn
                )
hard_dc_left = pinnjax.HardDirichletConstraint(
                domain, 
                condition=0.0, 
                side=(-1,)
                )
hard_dc_right = pinnjax.HardDirichletConstraint(
                domain,
                condition=0.0, 
                side=(1,)
                )

optimization = pinnjax.Optimization(
    input_transformation=pinnjax.NormalizationBetweenNeg1and1(domain=domain),
    output_transformation=None, 
    hard_constraint=(hard_ic, hard_dc_left, hard_dc_right), 
)

Since all three of these constraints are compatible with each other they will be combined.

Figure

Total Time    = 1m: 26.793s
Final Loss:
    Class:
        Diffusion = 0.00535355
        DiffusionBC = 3.7494e-31
        DiffusionIC = 0
    Type:
        PartialDifferentialEquation = 0.00535355
        BoundaryCondition = 3.7494e-31
        InitialCondition = 0

And, thus, here we achieve the best results so far.

docs.title: Problem Description
docs.text:
Wire-arc directed energy deposition is an additive manufacturing technique based on conventional welding technology, utilizing a robotic system for the layer-by-layer deposition of complex structures. However, the complex thermal dynamics inherent to the process present challenges in ensuring structural integrity and mechanical properties of fabricated components. Traditional methodologies, such as FEM, are capable of predicting thermal histories during deposition, but are prohibitively computationally expensive when dealing with the rapid, and repetitive simulations to determine optimal printing strategies.

Instead, let's surrogate the process using purely-Physics-informed Neural Networks.

The transient heat conduction problem is governed by the following equations:

\[ \begin{array}{c@{\qquad}l} \displaystyle \rho C_p \dfrac{\partial T}{\partial t} = k \nabla^2 T + Q_{\mathrm{goldak}}\left(\mathbf{x},t\right), & \mathbf{x} \in \Omega^\circ \\[1em] \displaystyle -k \dfrac{\partial T}{\partial n} = h\left(T-T_0\right) + \sigma\varepsilon \left(T^4-T_0^4\right), & \mathbf{x} \in \partial\Omega \setminus \Gamma_{-z} \\[1em] \displaystyle T(\mathbf{x},0) = T_0, & \mathbf{x} \in \Omega \\[1em] \displaystyle T(\mathbf{x},t) = T_0, & \mathbf{x} \in \Gamma_{-z} \end{array} \]

Where \(Q_{\mathrm{goldak}}\) refers to the volumetric heat flux most representative of wire-arc additive manufacturing, as defined in Goldak et al..

\[ Q_{\mathrm{goldak}} = \begin{cases} \dfrac{6\sqrt{3}\, f_f P \eta} {a_f b c \,\pi\sqrt{\pi}} \exp\left[ -3\left( \dfrac{x^2}{a_f^2} + \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} + \dfrac{z^2}{c^2} \right) \right], & x \leq 0, \\[1em] \dfrac{6\sqrt{3}\, f_r P \eta} {a_r b c \,\pi\sqrt{\pi}} \exp\left[ -3\left( \dfrac{x^2}{a_r^2} + \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} + \dfrac{z^2}{c^2} \right) \right], & x > 0. \end{cases} \]

Figure

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
If you play around with the parameters a bit and watch the losses during training you will come to realize that it can be difficult to know for certain how low the losses have to get to achieve 'decent' results. This is because the Residuals, at least the ones used here, are not normalized and thus the difference between the expected physics is absolute, not relative. By, simply modifying the material parameters will increase or decrease the loss. In the case of this example here losses as high as 1e18 are rather good. Therefore, it is useful to be able to compare our current predictions at runtime to something other than physics to get a better idea of how well our model is currently performing.

ground_truth = (
    pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parent / 
                            "_ground_truth" / 
                            PROJECT_NAME / 
                            "FEM_FC_3s.csv"
)
evaluation = pinnjax.SingleSpatialGridEvaluation.from_csv_file(
    ground_truth_path=ground_truth,
    # the model contains the `SpatialDomain`, 
    # but the `domain` can be provided instead.
    # if the `model` is provide we can evaluate the model 
    # against the `Evaluation` easier.
    model=model,  
    comparison_time=1.5,  # s
    csv_coordinate_column_order=[1, 2, 3, 0],  # to match [x, y, z, t]
    csv_truth_column=-1,
    regularity=100,
)

For this we have the 'true' solution, generated using traditional FEM methods, and saved to a .csv file. In this case, the columns are (t, x, y, z, T), so we use csv_coordinate_column_order to restructure the .csv. Then the rows span the entire spatial and temporal domain we are using here. It has also used the same the thermal material and goldak parameters, thus, if you modify those, the comparison will get worse, but that doesn't mean the model is training worse, just that its being compared to the wrong thing.

This particular Evaluation calculates RMSE, Relative L2, and R2, but we could change this by writing a child SingleSpatialGridEvaluation, a new evaluate() method, and updating the FORMAT, DICTIONARY, and METRIC_DIRECTION class variables.

The __call__() just calls evaluate(). Or, perhaps, a different, or entirely custom Evaluation is necessary for your purposes.

SingleSpatialGridEvaluation also includes a number of methods for plotting and slicing.

First, we could simply plot our evaluation at the provided comparison_time,

evaluation.plot()

Figure

Or, instead just a slice.

evaluation.plot(fixed_coordinates={"z": domain.max[2]})

Figure

Perhaps, we decide after the creation of evaluation that we would rather look at a different moment in time.

evaluation.update_truth_at(comparison_time=1.0)
evaluation.plot(fixed_coordinates={"z": domain.max[2]})

Figure

docs.title: Material Parameters
docs.text:
Enough visualization for now.

Quickly, let's define some material parameters for our problem.

goldak = pinnjax.Goldak(
    power=2.45e3,
    efficiency=0.9,
    width=0.006,
    front_ellipsoid_length=0.00257,
    rear_ellipsoid_length=0.006,
    depth=0.004,
    front_ellipsoid_distribution_factor=0.6,
    rear_ellipsoid_distribution_factor=1.4,
)

thermal_material = pinnjax.ThermalMaterial(
    heat_capacity=6.20e2,
    density=7.85e3,
    radiation_coefficient=0.2,
    thermal_conductivity=45,
    convection_coefficient=20,
    ambient_temperature=298,
    temperature_scale=5000,  # Scale-Factor
)

Both of these are just containers, which make future functions a bit simpler, in particular the Residuals we will define later.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
The next step is the model. Most of this was explained in previous examples, so I won't nearly be as verbose.

optimization: pinnjax.Optimization = pinnjax.Optimization(
    pinnjax.NormalizationBetweenNeg1and1(domain),  # input transformation
    pinnjax.ExpectedOutputRangeSoftplus(
        lower_bound=thermal_material.ambient_temperature, scale=thermal_material.temperature_scale
    ),  # output transformation
    (  # hard constraints
        pinnjax.HardScalarInitialConstraint(
            times=time,
            initial_condition=thermal_material.ambient_temperature,
        ),
        pinnjax.HardDirichletConstraint(
            domain=domain,
            condition=thermal_material.ambient_temperature,
            side=(0, 0, -1),
        ),
    ),
)

The HardConstraints are explained in detail in the 1D Diffusion example, but the ExpectedOutputRangeSoftplus (OutputTransformation) is new, so let's briefly explain it.

Neural Networks have been known to work best when the numbers, and therefore gradients remain smaller. This is part of the reason for the normalization of the inputs. However, in the case of WAAM, the expect temperature, range is much larger. Therefore, to take normalized inputs between -1 and 1 and output a temperature in the thousands, the weights have to be very large. To mitigate this, we try and scale our output towards the expected range. In the case of ExpectedOutputRangeSoftplus this transformation is:

  • transformed_output = lower_bound + scale * softplus(outputs).

The purpose of hyperparameter optimization is to modify the numerous parameters and factors involved in the training, such that the model reaches the global minimum, ideally, as fast as possible. However, in addition to 'going faster', it's also possible to reach your final destination faster by 'starting closer'.

This is the theory behind 'Weight Initialization'.

initialization = pinnjax.Initialization(
    weights=jinit.variance_scaling(
        scale=1.48**2,
        mode="fan_in",
        distribution="truncated_normal",  # proven best for GELU
    ),
    bias=jinit.zeros,
)

The pinnjax.Initialization, like some of the other attrs is just a container around the 'jax.nn.initializers', so you should look there for possible options and tips for choosing the ideal initialization. Here, as the note says, we use a variance-scaled version of the Kaiming Initialization, because it's been shown to work best with the Activation function we will use in a moment, GELU.

topology = (4, 64, 64, 64, 64, 1)  # depth: 4 - width: 64

Figure

activation = pinnjax.Activation(jax.nn.gelu, kwargs={"approximate": False})

Part of the reason we are using GELU, is because of the residuals we plan to solve in a moment. These residuals involve second-order derivatives of our output prediction. Therefore, it is important that our activation function is at least C2- smooth, and thus has continuous first- and second-order derivatives. That isn't to say that we must use GELU in these cases, but rather why we aren't using RELU, as was the case in the diffusion example.

And, once again, we use a FNN, and piece it all together.

model = pinnjax.FNN(
    domain,
    topology,
    activation,
    initialization=initialization,
    optimization=optimization,
)

docs.title: Residuals & Losses
docs.text:
The residuals used in this example are actually all currently included in PINN-JAX, however, it's unlikely you'll find personal use with them other than [DirichletBoundaryCondition][pinnjax.DirchletBoundaryCondition], which works as you'd expect.

If you'd like to know more about the inner workings of these classes, check the relevant documentation. However, it should be clear from the problem set up what physics each of these residuals are referring to.

pde = pinnjax.GoldakHeatFlux(thermal_material, goldak, path)
robin = pinnjax.RobinHeatFlux(thermal_material)
dirichlet = pinnjax.DirichletBoundaryCondition(
        condition=thermal_material.ambient_temperature
    )

The physical residuals are constructed from the governing equations detailed in the Problem Description by rearranging each equation into residual form such that the resulting expression is equal to zero.

From there, we take the MSE to calculate the loss.

\[ \mathcal{L}_{PDE} = \dfrac{1}{N_{PDE}} \sum_{i=1}^{N_{PDE}} \left| R_{PDE}\left(x_{PDE}^{i}, t_{PDE}^{i}\right) \right|^{2} \] \[ \mathcal{L}_{BC} = \dfrac{1}{N_{BC}} \sum_{i=1}^{N_{BC}} \left| R_{BC}\left(x_{BC}^{i}, t_{BC}^{i}\right) \right|^{2} \] 
pde = pinnjax.GoldakHeatFlux(thermal_material, goldak, path)
robin = pinnjax.RobinHeatFlux(thermal_material)
dirichlet = pinnjax.DirichletBoundaryCondition(
        condition=thermal_material.ambient_temperature
    )

The losses are then weighted and normalized, such that the mean is 1 as to avoid changing the overall loss scale:

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{L} &= \frac{ N\left( w_{\mathrm{BC}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BC}} + w_{\mathrm{PDE}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PDE}} \right) }{ w_{\mathrm{BC}} + w_{\mathrm{PDE}} } \\[1.0em] &\text{where } N \text{ is the number of weights.} \end{aligned} \] 
residual_functions: list[pinnjax.Residual] = [
    pde,
    robin,
    robin,
    robin,
    robin,
    dirichlet,
    robin,
    pde,  # added path residual -  `Box`
    robin,  # added path residual - `Rectangle`
]

geometry.assign_residuals(residual_functions)
geometry.assign_loss(pinnjax.ResidualMSError())

docs.title: Prediction
docs.text:
Since this is a 3D domain, we could of course compare against a 3D grid, however, we also can compare against a 2D domain, and take internal slices, which could be more informative than the pure 3D version

grid_2D = pinnjax.RectangularGrid2D(
    domain=updated_model.domain,
    fixed_coordinates={"z": float(domain.max[2])}, 
    num_points=(200, 100),
    time_range=(time.min, time.max),
    num_times=100,
)

To explain each of the parameters, we provide the whole 3D domain, but then fix one of the coordinates, similar to when we use .center(), this results in a 2D slide. We then want 200 points in the x direction, and 100 in the y direction. for 20.000 spatial points, and then 100 timesteps for a grand total of 2.000.000 spatial-temporal points, and thus model predictions.

Now simply just input the updated model and the Grid into predict_evolution().

predictions = pinnjax.predict_evolution(model_cpu, grid_2D)

And then plot the results.

pinnjax.plot_prediction_evolution(predictions, grid_2D)

We could also predict a single point using pinnjax.predict() and pinnjax.plot_prediction(). In that case, the Grid constructed wouldn't have needed its own temporal points, and instead a time scalar could be given to pinnjax.predict().

Figure

Next, we can plot the predictions at a number of points throughout the entire time domain. We can also compare the results directly against the .csv, by including the pathlib.Path to the .csv.

Note

This is planned to eventually work with Evaluation in general, but that isn't the case yet.

First, to select some points:

spatial_points = [
    [0.2, 0.5, 1.0],
    [0.7, 0.5, 1.0],
    [0.5, 0.5, 1.0],
    [0.3, 0.25, 1.0],
    [0.6, 0.75, 1.0],
]

pinnjax.value_over_time_plot(
    spatial_points=spatial_points,
    point_type="percentage",
    model=updated_model,
    truth=ground_truth,
    csv_coordinate_column_order=[1, 2, 3, 0],  # to match [x, y, z, t]
    csv_truth_column=-1,
    domain=domain,
    show_points=True, 
    x_axis_label="Time [s]",
    y_axis_label="Temperature [K]",
)

Because point_type = "percentage", as opposed to "coordinate", the spatial_points are interpreted as normalized fractions of the SpatialDomain. show_points=True visualizes that for us by generating a secondary plot showing the selected spatial_points within the domain.

Figure

Figure

Or instead of at particular points, but particular times. Looking instead at the whole Path at those time_instances.

time_instances = [0.6, 1.3, 2.2]  # s

pinnjax.value_along_path_plot(
    time_instances=time_instances,
    path=path,
    model=updated_model,
    domain=domain,
    truth=ground_truth,
    csv_coordinate_column_order=[1, 2, 3, 0],  # to match [x, y, z, t]
    csv_truth_column=-1,
    y_axis_label="Temperature [K]",
)

Figure
